Cyber Attack Disrupts Steel Industry Operations Across Mexico

A major cyber attack targeting several steel manufacturing firms in Mexico has disrupted production and logistics operations, threatening to ripple through the country’s vital construction and manufacturing supply chains. The incident, which began late Sunday night and continues at the time of writing, has been described by industry sources as “the most significant cyber event to impact Mexico’s steel sector in recent years.”

The attack, believed to involve ransomware deployed against core IT infrastructure, has forced at least three major steel producers—Grupo Aceros del Norte, AceroMex, and Laminados y Tuberías Pacifico—to halt or scale back production at facilities in Monterrey, Saltillo, and Veracruz. Officials from these companies confirmed that affected plants have been unable to process orders, issue shipping documentation, or access internal communications systems.

“We are working with cybersecurity experts and federal authorities to assess the extent of the breach and restore operations safely,” said Eduardo Martínez, CIO at Grupo Aceros del Norte. “At this moment, our priority is the integrity and safety of our employees, as well as protecting our customers’ data.”

According to the Mexican Steel Industry Association (AMIA), the attack has already led to an estimated 27% drop in daily steel output in the affected regions. “We are receiving reports from members that key production lines have been shut down as a precaution, and outbound shipments have been delayed indefinitely,” said AMIA president Laura Aguilar. “The situation is evolving rapidly, and the full impact on supply chains is not yet clear.”

Trade unions have voiced concern for workers at the impacted facilities. “Plant closures and IT outages have left thousands of employees in limbo,” said Carlos Mendoza, spokesperson for the National Steelworkers’ Federation. “We urge companies to provide clear communication and ensure that wages and benefits are not disrupted during this crisis.”

Local analysts warn that continued disruption could have significant consequences for downstream industries reliant on steel inputs. “If this persists for more than a week, construction projects and automotive manufacturing schedules across Mexico could face serious delays,” said Rogelio Ruiz, a metals sector analyst at Capital Mexicana Consultores.

While no group has claimed responsibility for the attack, cybersecurity experts note that the tactics bear hallmarks of recent ransomware campaigns targeting industrial firms worldwide. “Incidents like this underscore the urgent need for robust cybersecurity protocols in critical manufacturing sectors,” said Mariana Torres, director at CyberDefensa MX.

Federal cybersecurity authorities are assisting affected companies with investigation and recovery efforts. As of Tuesday afternoon, there is no timeline for full restoration of operations.
